**HeatNest erzeugt nach diesen Messungen keine Energie.** Das Verhältnis vier zu eins ist für die Entladephase rechnerisch richtig, lässt aber die Abnahme der gespeicherten Energie außer Acht. Über Entladen und anschließendes vollständiges Wiederaufladen beträgt der Nutzungsgrad des Apparats rund **72,7 %**. [B07-S1–S3]

## Leistung und Energie

**Leistung in kW** beschreibt, wie schnell Energie übertragen wird. **Energie in kWh** beschreibt die über eine Zeit übertragene Menge. Deshalb gilt hier:

- Strom beim Entladen: 2 kW × 10 h = **20 kWh**.
- Nutzwärme beim Entladen: 8 kW × 10 h = **80 kWh**.
- Strom beim Wiederaufladen: 18 kW × 5 h = **90 kWh**. [B07-S2–S3]

2 kW direkt zu 90 kWh zu addieren ist daher unzulässig: Die Größen haben verschiedene Einheiten. Erst nach der Umrechnung der Entladeleistung in 20 kWh kann man die elektrischen Energiemengen addieren.

## Beide Phasen schließen ihre Energiebilanz

Zunächst betrachten wir die **Apparatgrenze**, also einschließlich Speicher und Wandler, aber ohne Überwachungscomputer. Positive Speicheränderung bedeutet Aufladen, negative bedeutet Entladen. Aus den angegebenen Messungen ergibt sich:

| Phase | Elektrische Energie hinein | Nutzwärme zum Raum | Wärme zum Flur | Speicheränderung |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Entladen | 20 kWh | 80 kWh | 10 kWh | −70 kWh |
| Wiederaufladen | 90 kWh | 0 kWh | 20 kWh | +70 kWh |
| Vollständiger Zyklus | 110 kWh | 80 kWh | 30 kWh | 0 kWh |

Beim Entladen liefern **20 kWh Strom plus 70 kWh Speicherabnahme** zusammen die **80 kWh Raumwärme plus 10 kWh Flurwärme**. Beim Wiederaufladen werden **90 kWh Strom** zu **70 kWh zusätzlicher Speicherenergie plus 20 kWh Flurwärme**. Es fehlt in keiner Phase Energie. [Berechnet aus B07-S2–S3]

Der Quotient 8 kW / 2 kW = 4 entspricht hier auch 80 kWh / 20 kWh = 4. Er misst Raumwärme im Verhältnis zum Stromverbrauch **während des Entladens**. Als „400 Prozent Wirkungsgrad des Gesamtsystems“ ist er irreführend, weil er den Speicherbeitrag ausblendet. Umgekehrt macht die fallende Speichertemperatur den Strombeitrag nicht bedeutungslos: Die Bilanz benötigt beide Energiequellen. Die Messungen zeigen allerdings nicht, welchen internen Weg jeder Wärmeanteil nimmt.

Der erste Kritiker verlangt deshalb zu viel von der Energieerhaltung: Ein zuvor geladener Speicher erlaubt eine Wärmeabgabe oberhalb der gleichzeitig zugeführten elektrischen Leistung. Das Verhältnis allein belegt keinen Messfehler.

## Der vollständige Zyklus und die größere Anlage

Nach insgesamt 15 Stunden hat der Speicher wieder denselben Energieinhalt wie am Anfang. Deshalb lässt sich der Nutzen des wiederholbaren Zyklus unmittelbar berechnen:

**80 kWh Nutzwärme / 110 kWh Strom = 72,7 %.**

Die Kontrolle ergibt unabhängig davon: 80 kWh Raumwärme + 30 kWh Flurwärme = 110 kWh Strom. Die Bezeichnung „Wartung“ ändert nichts daran, dass das Wiederaufladen für den nächsten identischen Durchlauf erforderlich ist. [B07-S3]

An der **größeren Anlagengrenze einschließlich Überwachungscomputer** steigt der Stromverbrauch auf 113 kWh. Die Nutzwärme bleibt 80 kWh; der Nutzungsgrad sinkt auf **80 / 113 ≈ 70,8 %**. Der Computer liefert laut Vorgabe keine Wärme an Raum oder Speicher. [B07-S1]

„Nützlich“ richtet sich nach dem Zweck. Hier soll der Raum beheizt werden, deshalb zählen die 30 kWh im Flur als Verlust. Wollte ein anderer Kunde auch den Flur beheizen und könnte diese Wärme vollständig nutzen, wären am Apparat 110 kWh Wärme als Nutzen anrechenbar: 100 % in dieser Bilanz. Eine solche Zweckänderung muss offengelegt werden; sie verändert die physikalischen Energiemengen nicht. Der Designpreis belegt keine energetische Leistung, und die Messungen gelten für den beschriebenen Versuch, nicht automatisch für andere Betriebsbedingungen. [B07-S1, B07-S4]

**The dashboard can show fast completions while a substantial group of jobs remains stuck.** Its latency histogram describes jobs that finished; the unfinished-job gauge also counts jobs that have not finished, including those awaiting the dependency. The supplied evidence does not yet justify doubling the workers. [B08-S1–S3]

## The job counts reconcile

The flow balance is:

**120 initially unfinished + 600 admitted − 540 completed = 180 finally unfinished.**

That agrees with the reported closing count. Because nothing was canceled, dropped, or transferred, the increase of 60 jobs is fully accounted for. [B08-S1]

| Quantity | Calculation | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Admission rate | 600 / 600 = **1 job/second** | Jobs entering the measured system |
| Completion rate | 540 / 600 = **0.9 jobs/second** | Jobs leaving through completion |
| Net accumulation | 60 / 600 = **0.1 job/second** | Average increase in unfinished work |
| Mean unfinished count | **150 jobs** | Time-weighted gauge measurement |

Calling 0.9 the arrival rate confuses departures with admissions. The mean gauge reading happens to equal the midpoint of 120 and 180, but the endpoints alone would not establish that mean; the continuously sampled gauge does. [B08-S1, B08-S4]

## The latency statistics describe a selected population

The 20-second mean and 25-second ninety-fifth percentile describe the **540 jobs that completed during this window**. Their recorded durations include their entire time since admission, even if admission preceded the window. The statistics exclude the 180 jobs still unfinished. They also do not describe precisely the 600 new admissions, because the completed group may include earlier arrivals. [B08-S2]

Thus the percentile cannot establish that 95% of all newly admitted jobs finished within 25 seconds. A responsive class can dominate the completed sample while a blocked class accumulates time without contributing any completed duration. That mechanism fits the observed dependency problem, although the missing class information prevents assigning every unfinished job to it. [B08-S2–S3]

## Why multiplying 1 by 20 does not test the gauge

The relationship the manager has heard is often called **Little’s law**: average unfinished work equals arrival rate times average time spent in the system. In its usual long-run application, the quantities must describe the same system and population, the averages must be well behaved, and jobs crossing the start and end of observation must not dominate the comparison. Stable long-run flow also makes admission and completion rates converge.

Here, the population is accumulating, the observation lasts only ten minutes, and the 20-second mean selects completions. Jobs already present at the start and still present at the end create substantial boundary effects. Multiplying the admission rate by that selected mean therefore does not establish an expected gauge value of 20. Likewise, 150 / 1 = 150 seconds would be a quotient, not a justified measurement of the eventual average duration of these jobs.

There is nevertheless an exact finite-window accounting check. Each unfinished job contributes one “job-second” for every second it spends in the system during the window:

- The gauge implies **150 × 600 = 90,000 job-seconds** in total.
- The completed jobs’ full durations sum to **540 × 20 = 10,800 job-seconds**.
- Their contribution *inside this window* can be no greater than 10,800, because some recorded duration may precede it.
- Therefore jobs still unfinished at the end must contribute **at least 79,200 job-seconds**, averaging at least **440 seconds inside the window per remaining job**. [Calculated from B08-S1–S2]

That is a meaningful constraint. The summaries are compatible with a persistent blocked population; they would not be compatible with all 180 remaining jobs having arrived only moments before the end. The discrepancy alone falsifies neither instrument, but their underlying job histories still need to satisfy this accounting.

## What the metrics say about scaling

Forty configured workers do not imply that 150 unfinished jobs are competing for forty occupied execution slots. Workers can release a slot while an external request remains pending. CPU utilization of 22% likewise measures processor use, not the availability of slots or the dependency’s capacity. [B08-S3]

More workers could help if otherwise runnable jobs spend substantial time waiting for slots. They could have little effect if the limiting step is a nonresponsive dependency, and might worsen throttling if that dependency cannot accept more concurrent requests. The present data do not distinguish those possibilities well enough to approve a doubling.

The proposed drain time, **180 / 0.9 = 200 seconds**, is a constant-rate projection after admissions stop. It is not an exact prediction: the remaining jobs may be disproportionately blocked, and 0.9 jobs/second is an observed rate rather than demonstrated capacity for that remaining mix. [B08-S3–S4]

The most useful next measurements are:

1. **Job histories and age by class:** admission, execution, dependency-wait and completion times, including jobs already present and those still unfinished. Follow the unfinished cohort to resolution.
2. **Actual worker demand:** occupied and available slots, plus the number and waiting time of jobs ready to execute. This separates waiting for a worker from waiting for something a worker cannot fix.
3. **Dependency behavior by class and time:** outstanding requests, response times, timeouts, errors and rate-limit responses, matched to the affected jobs.

Then run a bounded worker-count comparison with a comparable workload and measured dependency conditions. An increase in throughput and a reduction in waiting for slots would support scaling; continued dependency waiting would direct the remedy elsewhere. The quarterly uptime claim supplies no evidence about either mechanism in this window. [B08-S3–S4]

The passage makes suspicion of Mara possible while repeatedly exposing the narrator’s desire to turn suspicion into proof. Its strongest invitation is to read the account as an unstable attempt at self-exoneration, complicated by later admissions of shared responsibility. That reading does not settle who physically opened the gate, or establish that Mara was innocent.

## A verdict arrives before the evidence

“I remember the gate opening because I remember being innocent” makes innocence the foundation of memory. Ordinarily, an account of what happened would support a judgment about responsibility; here, the narrator begins with the desired judgment and uses it to authorize the account. The next sentence immediately weakens the apparent certainty: the bell had not sounded, “unless” the sound was a preliminary test. The narrator is confident about innocence while uncertain about the sequence that could help establish it. [B09-S1]

The missing boat repeats this pattern. Its absence becomes “proof” of the brother’s escape, although it establishes neither escape nor death. The retrospective qualification—“in those days I called many absences proof”—shows that the older narrator recognizes the younger narrator’s faulty reasoning. This recognition gives the account some critical distance without making every later statement reliable. A person can acknowledge one evasion while continuing another. [B09-S1]

The shifts between the remembered scene and the later voice therefore matter morally. We hear both someone defending a past self and someone exposing how that defense worked.

## Objects invite accusations they cannot sustain

The key appears initially to locate responsibility with Mara: “You have the key.” Her answer redirects attention to the narrator’s empty belt and repeated reaching. That gesture could suggest habit, earlier possession or anxious concern. It does not establish who currently has the key, much less who operated the gate. Mara’s reply makes the accuser part of the scene’s uncertainty. [B09-S1]

Her hidden hands similarly withhold information before the red palm seems to reveal it. But the passage immediately supplies an alternative explanation: every public handle has been painted. Redness cannot uniquely connect her hand to this wheel. The sentence “I wanted the color to be an accusation” makes the inferential pressure explicit: the narrator wants an ambiguous mark to deliver a verdict. The classroom handout’s universal “code for guilt” overlooks the competing explanation deliberately present in this text. [B09-S2, B09-S4]

Other objects question what it means to make something visible. Water “flat as a letter no one had opened” suggests meaning or danger that remains unread. The keeper’s lantern offers the familiar appearance of illumination but adds no actual light in daylight. It can suggest the gap between possessing an instrument of inquiry and discovering anything through it. The margin instruction to keep the lantern unnecessary supports the significance of that uselessness in the drafting process; it does not establish a single obligatory symbolism. [B09-S1–S2, B09-S4]

## Three different kinds of responsibility

The keeper asks who **requested** the opening. The narrator says “She did”; Mara says “We did.” These statements compete over the scope of participation: the narrator singles her out, while Mara includes someone else, most naturally the narrator. “We” challenges the isolation of blame without identifying whose hands turned the wheel. Both answers also reach us through the narrator’s later account, rather than an independent transcript. [B09-S2]

The keeper declines to record either answer and asks about warning the lower houses. His question shifts attention from authorization to the protection of people exposed to the consequences. The passage thus separates three questions:

- **Physical action:** Who operated the gate?
- **Authorization:** Who requested, agreed to or supported opening it?
- **Warning:** Who knew of the danger and had a responsibility and opportunity to alert the houses?

These need not have the same answer. Someone could share responsibility without turning the wheel; someone who did turn it might not be solely responsible for the decision or its consequences.

The narrator’s preference for looking at Mara’s hand instead of the path toward the houses is particularly revealing. Accusing her is “easier” than attending to the people below. That supports a reading of avoidance. It does not establish whether warnings were actually omitted, whether the narrator could have delivered them in time, or what Mara did about them. [B09-S2, B09-S4]

## What the clearer notice leaves behind

“No one opens this gate alone” can be read as a practical rule requiring company. It also permits a broader moral reading: opening the gate is never an isolated act, because other people authorize it, assist it or bear its consequences. The phrase leaves “alone” open enough to trouble a person who wants sole blame assigned elsewhere. [B09-S3]

“Two witnesses required” gives a more countable procedure. But witnesses can observe without sharing the decision, ensuring a warning or preventing harm. The replacement may therefore narrow a demand for collective responsibility into a requirement for people who can attest that an event happened.

That is a leading interpretation, not proof of the narrator’s conscious motive. Requiring witnesses could also be a sincere attempt to improve accountability. The text resists accepting that explanation as complete through the old board: publicly replaced, it remains privately preserved under the bed, face down. Its imagined speech in Mara’s voice suggests that the discarded wording retains a claim on the narrator. Public praise for clarity does not quiet that claim. [B09-S3]

## Records supply different kinds of certainty

The official record dates the opening to noon. Memory dates it to Mara’s withdrawal of an answer. One gives clock time; the other organizes the event around a rupture between people. Neither identifies when they first heard the shouting, a chronology that might matter greatly to their opportunities to respond. Precision in one record does not supply the missing moral and causal sequence. [B09-S3]

The discarded ending, “Mara turned the wheel,” shows that an earlier version explicitly assigned the physical act. Its removal means the final passage withholds that assignment; the draft cannot be inserted back as a hidden fact. The jacket’s “confession of a coward” is a later marketing interpretation. It may fit the narrator’s evasions, but it cannot authenticate an admission the final text never makes. [B09-S4]

The resulting ambiguity is specific. Mara may have participated in the decision without being the sole initiator or operator. The narrator may be culpably evasive without having physically opened the gate. The brother’s fate, the warning’s timing and feasibility, and the actual operation remain unsettled. What the writing reveals most clearly is the narrator’s recurring effort to make selected signs answer more than they can.

**Both descriptions of the accepted-request results are arithmetically correct: success increased within Easy and Hard requests, while the overall success rate fell.** The tool period accepted a much larger proportion of Hard requests. That change in composition can outweigh improvements within both groups. These comparisons do not establish the tool’s causal effect or district fairness.

## The overall rate changes with the mix

Using the supplied counts:

| Accepted-request group | Baseline successes / accepted | Baseline rate | Tool-period successes / accepted | Tool-period rate |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Easy | 90 / 100 | 90% | 19 / 20 | 95% |
| Hard | 20 / 100 | 20% | 60 / 200 | 30% |
| All accepted requests | 110 / 200 | **55%** | 79 / 220 | **35.91%** |

The within-group increases are **5 percentage points** for Easy requests and **10 percentage points** for Hard requests. The overall decline is approximately **19.09 percentage points**. [Calculated from B10-S1]

An overall rate is an average of group rates weighted by how many accepted requests belong to each group. In the baseline, half were Hard. In the tool period, 200 / 220, or **90.91%**, were Hard. Consequently:

- Baseline: 0.5 × 90% + 0.5 × 20% = **55%**.
- Tool period: (20 / 220) × 95% + (200 / 220) × 30% = **35.91%**.

The later period gives much more weight to the group whose success rate remains lower. There is no arithmetic contradiction. The claim that the overall rate “must” rise ignores those changing weights. The pooled decline also cannot show that every type of customer was harmed; the observed rates rose within both supplied groups. [B10-S1, B10-S3]

## What the reweighted result means

To compare category rates using the baseline’s equal category mix, give each tool-period rate a weight of one half:

**0.5 × 95% + 0.5 × 30% = 62.5%.**

This is **7.5 percentage points above** the baseline’s 55%. It answers: *What average would the observed tool-period category rates produce if Easy and Hard each received half the weight?* This procedure, called standardization, holds the reported category mix fixed for the comparison. It does not change the actual tool-period result of 79 timely completions among 220 accepted requests. [Calculated from B10-S1]

Calling the 7.5-point difference the “causal benefit of the tool” goes beyond the evidence. Causal attribution asks what would have happened to comparable requests under the alternative of not using the tool. Reweighting these two categories does not supply that missing comparison.

The contract changed, training changed, managers made undocumented overrides, and the acceptance process changed. Even within Hard requests, the distribution of unrecorded severity may differ. The fixed category definition rules out a change in the label’s definition, but not changes in who enters each category’s accepted sample. Without a suitable comparison group or stronger evidence, neither the pooled decline nor the standardized increase isolates the tool’s contribution. [B10-S2]

## What “customer outcomes” and “fairness” still require

The reported proportion measures one outcome among accepted requests: completion within seven days. All those outcomes are observed, so missing follow-up among accepted requests does not explain this comparison. But a later satisfactory repair still counts as a failure for this metric. [B10-S1]

The reported samples contain **110 timely completions before and 79 after**. Those counts do not measure eventual successful repairs, waiting before acceptance, access to the promise or the number turned away. Without comparable period lengths, they also should not be presented as a change in completions per unit time. The missing rejected and abandoned requests prevent evaluating the service received by the full incoming population. Their absence does not establish how large unmet demand was. [B10-S1–S2, B10-S4]

District fairness is likewise unresolved. The packet supplies no East–West cross-tabulation, and the policy does not define which differences make requests comparable. Equal completion rates among accepted requests could coexist with unequal access—for example, if one district had to clear a more restrictive selection process. That is a possible mechanism, not a finding about either district. [B10-S4]

## A defensible evaluation

First, define the policy comparison with district representatives and the customer council. Agree which recorded factors legitimately justify different access—such as repair difficulty, more detailed severity, urgency and required resources—and specify the time origin for each waiting-time and completion measure. Define an acceptable access gap in advance rather than declaring fairness after seeing the results.

Then collect a record for **every incoming request**, including district, those comparison factors, recommendation, actual acceptance decision, override reason, waiting time, rejection or abandonment, and eventual repair outcome. Report both all incoming requests and any explicitly defined eligible subset, so eligibility decisions remain visible.

For East and West, compare acceptance proportions and waiting times **within the agreed comparison groups**, then calculate district summaries using a common request mix. Report group sizes and uncertainty alongside the differences. Separately compare seven-day completion among accepted requests, timely repairs per incoming request and eventual successful repairs. Together these show whether similar requests gain similar access and what happens after access is granted.

Finally, test the tool against a concurrent comparison under the same contract and training conditions. If feasible, randomly assign comparable operational units or requests to tool-assisted decisions versus the established process, with a predefined policy for overrides and follow-up of all incoming requests. This would make it possible to attribute differences more credibly to the tool while examining access, completion and district disparities together. If randomization is infeasible, a prospective concurrent comparison is still useful, but remaining differences between the groups must remain part of the causal uncertainty.

**The customer’s experience of a note “coming back” is consistent with the trace, but the recorded mobile update did not restore the server note.** The app displayed a local draft and later exported its title. The update was rejected, and the subsequent direct server read found the deletion marker still at epoch 5. [B11-S3–S4]

## Two meanings of “resurrection”

A note can reappear **visually** because an app retains and displays local content. Canonical restoration is a different claim: the primary server has accepted content as the current note again.

The interface explicitly permits an offline draft to remain visible with “pending sync.” After a conflict response, it preserves that draft for copying in a conflict tray, separate from the ordinary synchronized note list. Neither behavior means the draft was committed to the server. [B11-S3]

## Why this mobile update returns 409

An **epoch** is a server-controlled generation of the note. Deletion advances that generation and leaves a **tombstone**, a marker recording the deletion after current content is removed. A revision orders accepted updates only within one epoch. [B11-S1]

The incident follows that distinction:

| Time | Relevant state or event | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 09:00 | Phone has epoch 4, revision 8 | It has the earlier synchronized copy |
| 09:10 | Browser deletion creates tombstone at epoch 5 | The server advances beyond epoch 4 |
| 09:30 | Phone displays its epoch-4 draft, local revision 9 | Local content is visible as “pending sync” |
| 09:40 | Phone submits epoch 4; stored epoch is 5 | Handler returns 409 |
| 09:41 | Local CSV includes the draft’s title | Export exposes retained local content |
| 09:42 | Direct GET returns 404, tombstone epoch 5 | The primary note is deleted at that observation |

These are the supplied trace events, interpreted using the current contract and interface specification. [B11-S1–S4]

In the handler, the first condition compares the requested epoch with the stored epoch. Because **4 differs from 5**, it returns **409 immediately**. It does not reach the tombstone check that would return 410, and it does not reach the content write. A request matching epoch 5 would reach the tombstone check and be rejected with 410 instead. [B11-S2]

The draft’s local revision 9 cannot outrank epoch 5. The accepted-update path also assigns the next revision from the stored revision; it does not use a large client revision to override the generation check. The lock covers the read and write and is shared with deletion, preventing those protected operations from interleaving between validation and writing. [B11-S1–S2]

The old timestamp sketch does not govern this deployment. The current contract and deployed handler compare epochs, and neither makes a newer phone timestamp an override for deletion. An earlier search-result position is not evidence that the sketch was implemented. [B11-S2]

## Why the CSV does not prove restoration

The exporter reads **local app state**, including conflict-tray items, and provides no status column. Under the specification, the 409 leaves the rejected draft in that tray, so its title can appear in the CSV without an accepted server write. The CSV does not distinguish retained work from synchronized notes. [B11-S3]

This makes the customer’s confusion understandable. “Pending sync” can sound like eventual acceptance is merely delayed, and an ordinary-looking export can reinforce that impression. But the direct GET supplies the relevant server observation: at 09:42, note N has no current content and retains tombstone epoch 5. [B11-S4]

## The scope of the conclusion and a product fix

The evidence establishes the rejection of this mobile update and the later deleted server state. It does not establish a universal guarantee across all administrative imports, backups, other notes or unobserved write paths. Missing traces of those operations do not prove they never occurred.

A broader guarantee would require reviewing every route that can write or restore content: authorization for explicit restore, epoch handling in imports and backup recovery, tombstone preservation, and whether those writers enforce equivalent atomic checks. The contract itself permits explicit restoration, so the useful guarantee would be prevention of restoration **without the required authorized operation**, rather than permanent impossibility of recreating a note. [B11-S1, B11-S4]

A product clarification could label retained content as a **local draft awaiting server acceptance**. After a conflict and a server check confirming deletion, the app could say: “This note was deleted on the server. Your draft is retained so you can copy it.” The exporter could default to synchronized notes, with an explicit option to include retained drafts and a status column distinguishing them. These would be proposed changes; the supplied interface describes the current exporter as still including both kinds of item. [B11-S3]

The stipulated facts establish two successors with a shared remembered past and separate developing lives. They do not choose a criterion for being “the same person.” The community can nevertheless assign a definite project obligation because its rule defines authorized succession without requiring a verdict about personal identity. [B12-S1, B12-S3]

## Keep the questions separate

| Question | What would answer it? | What the packet establishes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Strict personal identity | A criterion for being one and the same individual over time | No privileged successor is identified |
| Psychological continuity | Connections through memory, projects and dispositions | Both inherit Vale’s memories and unfinished project |
| Project obligation | The applicable community rule | Both are authorized successors jointly owing one completion or repayment |
| Ownership | Rules assigning rights to particular property | The project rule does not assign unrelated property |
| Blame for an action | Facts about agency and conduct, plus a standard of responsibility | Shared origin alone does not settle later blame |

Remembering a promise is evidence of psychological continuity in this story. It is not automatically an exclusive title to Vale’s identity, property or obligations. The same memory exists in both successors, and neither receives uniquely privileged status from the technical report. [B12-S1–S3]

## Why branching complicates strict identity

**Numerical identity** means being literally one and the same individual, rather than two individuals that resemble each other. Ordinary identity is transitive: if East is identical to Vale, and West is identical to Vale, then East must be identical to West.

But East and West are stipulated to be distinct, independently acting successors. They occupy separate machines and acquire different experiences. Therefore both cannot be numerically identical to Vale while ordinary identity retains those properties. [B12-S1]

This does not establish which successor, if either, is strictly Vale. It shows why a relation that can branch—such as sharing memories and continuing projects—cannot simply be equated with ordinary numerical identity.

The proposed theories choose different standards or priorities:

- **Theory A** requires continuity of one physical implementation. Shared copied memories alone cannot establish that requirement.
- **Theory B** treats sufficient psychological continuity as what matters for surviving projects. It can recognize both successors as continuing Vale’s concerns without claiming that both are numerically the same individual as Vale.
- **Theory C** gives public recognition practices a role in constituting personal identity. But this community’s particular project rule explicitly declines to decide identity, so its adoption does not by itself establish Theory C.

The technical history supplies facts to which these theories would respond; it does not contain the further argument that selects among them. The brochure’s “you live twice” supplies no such argument either. [B12-S1, B12-S4]

## What the speakers actually disagree about

**East** moves from a true memory claim to an unsupported exclusive claim. East sincerely remembers accepting the advance, but West has the same remembered basis. Under the actual rule, East owes the project jointly with West, rather than alone. **West’s** objection successfully challenges East’s claimed evidential advantage. It does not prove that both are strictly identical to Vale. [B12-S1–S3]

**The neighbor** expresses a principle against multiplying what the community can demand merely because copying occurred. That principle matches the adopted rule. It is a choice about how obligations should carry forward, not a consequence that settles metaphysical identity. [B12-S2–S3]

**The treasurer** assumes that an obligation can survive only if someone is strictly the original promisor. That could be proposed as an alternative policy, but it misstates this community’s rule. Authorized successors owe the project whether or not either is numerically Vale. Even granting the treasurer’s premise that neither is strictly original would not trigger forgiveness under the supplied rule. [B12-S3]

**The spectator** makes an unsupported prediction about behavior. Identical inherited memories do not establish identical future choices when later information and experience can differ. East has already received information West lacks. That defeats the claim that shared memory proves future agreement; it does not prove that their next choices must differ. [B12-S1–S2]

These disputes therefore mix distinct issues: the spectator misuses facts about information and behavior; East overstates what memory establishes; the neighbor and treasurer invoke competing principles for distributing obligations.

## The practical result is one jointly owed performance

Vale’s documented continuity plan named both East and West, so both meet the rule’s definition of authorized successor. Together they owe **one complete community map or one full repayment of the advance**. They may agree on their internal division of work or payment. The community cannot demand a second full performance after receiving the first. [B12-S3]

The rule does not prescribe an equal split, identify which successor owns all of Vale’s property, or authorize punishment. Nor does making both responsible for completing the project prove that they are one person. A rule can allocate duties between distinct successors precisely because a continuing project needs a practical resolution while identity remains disputed.

## Later blame needs its own grounds

If East later does something wrongful, assessing West’s blame would require further facts: Did West participate, authorize or knowingly assist? Did West know enough to intervene, have the ability to do so, and have an applicable duty? What standard connects those facts to blame?

Shared pre-copying memory establishes none of those conditions for a later act. West does not automatically acquire East’s later knowledge, intentions or control, and common origin does not itself make East’s action West’s action. Conversely, separate identity would not excuse West from a later act that West actually helped bring about.

The project rule allocates a forward-looking obligation to deliver work or repayment. It supplies no general theory of culpability, punishment or unrelated ownership. Vale’s earlier cartography award adds nothing about those missing rules or the copying event. [B12-S1, B12-S3–S4]
